title.en: Gimjang Day: Sharing Kimchi, Singing Arirang

summaryEn: As winter comes, Hoya helps relatives and neighbors make and share kimchi for gimjang (UNESCO 2013), then hears Arirang, the folk song shared across Korea (South Korea's UNESCO entry, 2012).
hoyaIntroEn: Winter is coming! Let's make kimchi with neighbors and hear a song shared across Korea.
hoyaOutroEn: Making kimchi together and singing Arirang: sharing makes it special!
learningGoalsEn: Understand why families made gimjang kimchi and that sharing is at its heart.
Know the yearly preparation for gimjang and the main ingredients (napa cabbage, chili powder, garlic, ginger, green onions).
Know that Arirang is a folk song with many regional versions, and that UNESCO inscribed gimjang (2013) and South Korea's Arirang (2012); North Korea's Arirang has its own separate listing.
Read and recognize 김장 (gimjang), 김치 (gimchi), 배추 (baechu), 고춧가루 (gochutgaru), 나눔 (nanum) and 아리랑 (arirang).

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

keywords.en: Kimchi and Gimjang Culture (the Korea Heritage Service's name for the UNESCO listing)

scenes.narrationEn: Brrr! Late autumn is turning to winter, {kw:gyeoul}. Hoya visits a busy yard. Long ago, fresh vegetables were hard to find in winter, so families made lots of kimchi at once. This is called gimjang.
scenes.captionEn: Making lots of kimchi before winter
scenes.artBrief: A hanok courtyard in late autumn with bare trees, stacks of napa cabbages and big clay jars; Hoya in a warm vest arriving with a basket.

art.altEn: Hoya arrives in a village yard as winter nears, with napa cabbages piled up and big kimchi jars waiting for gimjang.

scenes.narrationEn: Gimjang takes months of preparation! In spring, families get shrimp and anchovies for salting. In summer, they buy sea salt. In late summer, red chili peppers are dried and ground into chili powder.
scenes.artBrief: Three small seasonal panels: spring jars of salted tiny shrimp, summer sacks of white sea salt, late-summer red chili peppers drying on mats in the sun.

art.altEn: Gimjang starts months early: jars for salted shrimp, a basket of sea salt and a basket of dried red chili peppers.

scenes.narrationEn: On gimjang day, relatives and neighbors, {kw:iut}, come to help. They salt napa cabbages, then rub in a seasoning made with chili powder, garlic, ginger and green onions.
scenes.artBrief: Neighbors in aprons and rubber gloves around big basins, rubbing red seasoning between cabbage leaves; garlic, ginger and green onions nearby; Hoya helping.

art.altEn: Neighbors gather for gimjang and rub red seasoning into salted napa cabbages, and Hoya helps.

scenes.narrationEn: Every region makes kimchi its own way. In the cold north it is often milder and less salty; in the south it is saltier, with a redder, richer seasoning. So there are countless kinds of kimchi!
scenes.artBrief: A simple map-shaped table runner (no labels) with bowls of pale and deep-red kimchi placed from top to bottom; Hoya comparing two bowls.

art.altEn: Hoya compares two tables of kimchi: a milder, paler kind from the cold north and a saltier, redder kind from the south.

scenes.narrationEn: On gimjang day, the host family traditionally serves the helpers boiled pork with the cabbage's yellow inner leaves. Many families give kimchi to neighbors, too. Working together and sharing are the heart of gimjang.
scenes.artBrief: Helpers seated around a low table with sliced boiled pork and pale yellow cabbage leaves; a child carrying a covered dish of kimchi to the house next door; Hoya waving.

art.altEn: Helpers share boiled pork and cabbage leaves after gimjang, a child heads off to give kimchi next door, and Hoya waves.

scenes.narrationEn: In 2013, UNESCO added gimjang, making and sharing kimchi, to its heritage list. In Korean, the Heritage Service calls this listing {kw:gimchiwa-gimjangmunhwa}.

keyword.en: Kimchi and Gimjang Culture (the Korea Heritage Service's name for the UNESCO listing)

scenes.artBrief: Rows of filled clay kimchi jars glowing in late-afternoon light, with Hoya proudly holding a heritage card showing cabbage and hands.

art.altEn: Rows of filled kimchi jars glow in the late-afternoon sun, and Hoya cheers: gimjang is on UNESCO's heritage list.

scenes.narrationEn: As the day ends, Grandma hums a song known all over Korea: 'Arirang, arirang, arariyo…' Arirang is a folk song made and passed down by ordinary people over many generations.
scenes.artBrief: Grandma resting on the wooden porch at dusk, humming with eyes closed, musical notes drifting toward mountain ridges; Hoya leaning on her shoulder.

art.altEn: As the day ends Grandma rests and hums Arirang, a folk song known all over Korea, with Hoya close beside her.

scenes.narrationEn: Arirang has many versions. Regions have their own, like Jeongseon, Jindo and Miryang Arirang, and anyone can make up new verses! In 2012, UNESCO added South Korea's Arirang to its heritage list. North Korea's Arirang is listed separately.
scenes.artBrief: A winding mountain pass with three small scenes along it (mountain valley, island coast, river town), each with people singing; Hoya walking the path.

art.altEn: Hoya waves beside a winding mountain path past little groups of people, each singing their own Arirang.

checks.promptEn: Why did families make lots of kimchi at once for gimjang?

options.en: Fresh vegetables were hard to find in winter
Cabbage only grows in the cold north
Kimchi had to be ready before the new year
Kimchi jars were needed for a holiday feast

checks.explainEn: Fresh vegetables were hard to get in winter, so families made lots of kimchi at once to last through the winter.

checks.promptEn: What is at the heart of gimjang?

options.en: Making kimchi as fast as possible

checks.explainEn: Cooperation and sharing are the spirit of gimjang. Homes even exchange kimchi with each other.

checks.promptEn: Which statement about Arirang is true?

options.en: It has only one version everywhere
It was written by one famous composer
It is sung only in winter

checks.explainEn: Arirang has many regional versions, like Jeongseon, Jindo and Miryang Arirang, and anyone can make new lyrics.

facts.claimEn: Because fresh vegetables were hard to get in winter, families made a large amount of kimchi at once in late autumn to early winter to last through the winter; this custom is gimjang (UNESCO: Kimjang).
facts.claimKo: 겨울철에는 신선한 채소를 구하기 어려워 늦가을·초겨울에 겨우내 먹을 김치를 한꺼번에 많이 담갔으며, 이를 김장이라 한다.

facts.claimEn: Gimjang preparation takes months (more than half a year, per the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture) and runs through the year: in spring, families buy shrimp, anchovy and other seafood to salt; in summer, they buy sea salt; and in late summer, they dry red chili peppers and grind them into powder.
facts.claimKo: 김장 준비에는 반년 이상이 걸리며 1년 주기로 이어진다. 봄에는 새우·멸치 등 해산물을 구해 젓갈을 담그고, 여름에는 소금을 사며, 늦여름에는 고추를 말려 가루를 낸다.

sources.title: Kimjang, making and sharing kimchi in the Republic of Korea
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘Preparation follows a yearly cycle.’ / ‘In spring, households procure shrimp, anchovy and other seafood for salting and fermenting.’ / ‘In summer, they buy sea salt for the brine.’ / ‘In late summer, red chilli peppers are dried and ground into powder.’

sources.title: 김장
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘김장은 봄철의 젓갈담그기에서 초가을의 고추·마늘의 준비, 김장용 채소의 재배 등 준비하는 데에 반년 이상이 걸리는 한 가정의 큰 행사이었다.’

facts.claimEn: Relatives and neighbors help one another with gimjang: vegetables such as napa cabbage are salted, then mixed with a seasoning that includes chili powder, garlic, ginger and green onions.
facts.claimKo: 김장은 서로 도와가며 했으며, 배추 등 채소를 소금에 절인 뒤 고춧가루·마늘·생강·파 등이 든 양념을 버무린다.

sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘서로 도와가며 김장을 하는 풍속이 있었다.’ / ‘미나리·갓·마늘·파·생강·고춧가루와 같은 향미가 있는 채소가 부재료로 이용되고, 소금·젓갈이 간을 맞추기 위하여 사용된다.’

facts.claimEn: Kimchi differs by region: in the cold north it is typically less salty with milder seasoning, while in the south it is saltier with a redder, stronger seasoning; there are countless local varieties.
facts.claimKo: 김치는 지역마다 달라, 추운 북쪽은 싱겁고 담백하게, 남쪽은 짜고 빨갛고 진한 양념으로 담그며, 지역별 종류가 매우 많다.

sources.title: 김장

sources.title: 국가무형유산 김치 담그기
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘the countless local varieties of kimchi are a stellar example of cultural diversity.’

facts.claimEn: On gimjang day the host family traditionally boiled pork and served it with the cabbage's yellow inner leaves and seasoning to the helpers (a custom the Encyclopedia says is still kept as a fond tradition); kimchi is also exchanged among households, and cooperation and sharing are the spirit of gimjang.
facts.claimKo: 김장하는 날 집주인은 전통적으로 돼지고기를 삶아 배추의 노란 속잎과 양념을 일하는 사람들에게 내었고(속대쌈, 지금도 미풍으로 전해진다), 김치를 서로 나누기도 한다. 협동과 나눔이 김장 문화의 핵심이다.

facts.claimEn: Arirang is a widely shared Korean folk song, created and passed down orally by ordinary people over generations, built around a sung refrain such as 'Arirang, arirang, arariyo'; scholars offer several theories about where the refrain word comes from, but the refrain itself is treated as sung syllables that lift the mood and fill out the melody.
facts.claimKo: 아리랑은 구전으로 전승·재창조되어 온 한국의 대표 민요로, ‘아리랑 아리랑 아라리요’ 같은 후렴(여음)을 지닌다. 후렴어의 어원에는 여러 설이 있으나, 후렴은 흥을 돕고 음조를 메워 나가는 사설로 본다.

authorNotes: Spelling: RR for 김장/김치 is gimjang/gimchi. UNESCO's official title uses 'Kimjang', and 'kimchi' is the usual English word. The narration uses 'gimjang' and 'kimchi'; UNESCO's spelling 'Kimjang' stays in f1, f6 and the Sources screen (review 2026-10-11: the spoken aside was removed). Grandma humming Arirang at the end of the day is a story moment. The narration does not claim Arirang is a gimjang work song. The sources don't link the two, though some Arirang types are work songs (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture). The refrain quoted is the widely known one. The Encyclopedia notes the best-known 'Arirang' (경기/본조 아리랑) is a new folk-song (신민요) form; traditional regional ones include Jeongseon, Jindo and Miryang. Left out on purpose: UNESCO's estimate of 'some 3,600 variations'. Only one authoritative source for it was found, so it isn't in the narration. Also left out: theories about what 'Arirang' means (folk etymology), the DPRK listings (Arirang 2014; kimchi-making 2015), and the old practice of burying kimchi jars in the ground. National designations: 아리랑 (2015-09-22) and 김치 담그기 (2017-11-15) are National Intangible Heritage per the 국가유산포털. They aren't used in the narration.
